category.title: Range Query Data Structures
category.description: Advanced Range Query data structures including Segment Trees, Lazy Propagation, Fenwick Trees (BIT), and Sparse Tables.

algorithms.title: Segment Tree (Range Sum Query & Point Update)
algorithms.summary: Tree data structure for querying sum in any range [L, R] and updating point values in O(log N) logarithmic time.
explanation: 1. Binary tree where leaf nodes represent array elements and internal nodes store sum of child ranges.
2. Build Tree: Recursively divide array into halves down to leaves in O(N).
3. Range Query: Traverse subtrees overlapping query range [L, R] in O(log N).
4. Point Update: Traverse path from root to leaf, updating values along the path in O(log N).

exampleTrace.title: Trace arr = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], Query Range [1, 3]
traceSteps: Root covers [0..5] (sum=36) -> Split left [0..2] and right [3..5].
Left node covers [1..2] (sum=8). Right node covers [3..3] (sum=7).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Performs dynamic range queries and point updates in O(log N) time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When array elements change dynamically while answering range aggregate queries.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Database range indexes, financial order book total volume queries.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces slow O(N) array scans with logarithmic O(log N) tree operations.

algorithms.title: Segment Tree (Range Min & Max Queries)
algorithms.summary: Find minimum or maximum element in any arbitrary range [L, R] dynamically.
explanation: 1. Tree nodes store `min` or `max` value of left and right child subtrees.
2. Internal node merges children: `tree[node] = min(tree[2*node+1], tree[2*node+2])`.
3. Range Query: Returns `infinity` (for min) or `-infinity` (for max) when out of bounds.
4. Point Update: Updates leaf node and rebalances parent min/max up to the root.

exampleTrace.title: Trace arr = [2, 5, 1, 4, 9, 3], Query Min in [1, 4]
traceSteps: Tree stores range minima at each node.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes dynamic Range Minimum Query (RMQ) and Range Maximum Query.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding dynamic min/max over updating intervals.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Game leaderboard score dynamic boundaries, stock price trough detection.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(log N) query time instead of O(N) linear scans.

algorithms.title: Segment Tree (Range GCD Queries)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log(Max)) Build, O(log N * log(Max)) Query
algorithms.summary: Compute Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of elements in any range [L, R] with dynamic point updates.
explanation: 1. Internal node combines child GCD values: `tree[node] = gcd(tree[2*node+1], tree[2*node+2])`.
2. Identity element for GCD is 0 (`gcd(a, 0) = a`).
3. Range Query: Intersects query interval [L, R] and accumulates GCD recursively.
4. Enables dynamic updates where updating single array element re-computes GCD bounds in logarithmic time.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes dynamic Greatest Common Divisor over updating array intervals.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding GCD of dynamic subarrays in competitive programming.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Signal frequency analysis, lattice grid scale synchronization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(log N * log(Max)) dynamic query instead of O(N log(Max)).

algorithms.title: Segment Tree with Lazy Propagation (Range Update & Range Query)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log N) Range Update, O(log N) Range Query
algorithms.summary: Executes Range Updates [L, R] += val in O(log N) by deferring update operations to lazy array until children are accessed.
explanation: 1. Problem without Lazy: Updating range [L, R] takes O(N log N) if we update every node individually.
2. Lazy Propagation Idea: Mark internal nodes with pending updates (`lazy[node] += val`). Defer pushing to children until necessary.
3. Node Push: When visiting node `i`, apply pending `lazy[i]` to `tree[i]` and pass lazy tags down to child nodes `2*i+1` and `2*i+2`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Range Update [1..3] += 5 on array size 8
traceSteps: Tree node covering range [1..3] gets lazy tag += 5.
Tree node sum instantly updated by `(end - start + 1) * 5`.
Children are NOT updated immediately (O(log N) operations saved!).
Subsequent queries push lazy values down on-demand.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Performs dynamic Range Additions/Updates and Range Sum/Min Queries in O(log N) time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When updating entire contiguous array sub-ranges repeatedly.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Mass canvas pixel updates, bulk stock dividend updates across portfolios.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Avoids updating subtrees immediately, reducing range update complexity from O(N) to O(log N).

algorithms.title: Fenwick Tree / Binary Indexed Tree (Point Update & Prefix/Range Query)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log N) Build, O(log N) Query/Update
algorithms.summary: Lightweight 1-indexed array structure supporting point updates and prefix sum queries in O(log N) time with low constant overhead.
explanation: 1. Bit trick: `LSB(x) = x & (-x)`. `tree[i]` stores sum of range `(i - LSB(i), i]`.
2. Point Update `add(idx, val)`: Add `val` to `tree[idx]` and move to parent index `idx += idx & (-idx)`.
3. Prefix Query `query(idx)`: Accumulate `tree[idx]` and move to lower sub-range `idx -= idx & (-idx)`.
4. Range Query `[L, R]`: Computed instantly as `query(R) - query(L - 1)`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Fenwick Tree [1..6] Query Range [2, 4]
traceSteps: Prefix Sum(4) = query(4) (adds tree[4] which covers 1..4).
Range Sum [2..4] = Prefix Sum(4) - Prefix Sum(1).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes dynamic prefix sums and range sums with minimal code and high cache locality.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When implementing cumulative frequency tables, inversion counting, or dynamic rank queries.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Inversion count calculation, order statistic trees, competitive programming range queries.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Requires only O(N) memory array without tree pointers or recursion overhead.

algorithms.title: Fenwick Tree Range Update & Point/Range Query
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(log N) Range Update, O(log N) Range Query
algorithms.summary: Dual Fenwick Tree technique supporting Range Additions [L, R] += val and Range Queries in logarithmic time.
explanation: 1. Difference Array + BIT: Maintain two BITs (`B1` and `B2`).
2. Range Add `[L, R] += v`: `B1.update(L, v)`, `B1.update(R + 1, -v)`, `B2.update(L, v * (L - 1))`, `B2.update(R + 1, -v * R)`.
3. Prefix Sum Formula: `PrefixSum(x) = B1.query(x) * x - B2.query(x)`.
4. Range Query `[L, R] = PrefixSum(R) - PrefixSum(L - 1)`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Range Update [2, 4] += 3 on array size 6
traceSteps: Prefix sum query formula computes range addition dynamically in O(log N).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Performs Range Updates and Range Queries using simple BIT structures.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When Segment Tree is too heavy/verbose and range updates are required.
wAnswers.whereUsed: High performance competitive programming range update tasks.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(log N) operations with minimal memory footprint compared to Segment Trees.

algorithms.title: Sparse Table (Static Range Minimum Query - RMQ)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log N) Precomputation, O(1) Query
algorithms.summary: Precomputes powers-of-two range minima enabling instant O(1) constant time queries for static arrays.
explanation: 1. Sparse Table definition: `table[i][j]` stores minimum in range `[i, i + 2^j - 1]`.
2. Precomputation: `table[i][j] = min(table[i][j-1], table[i + 2^(j-1)][j-1])`.
3. Idempotent Query: Range [L, R] length `len = R - L + 1`. Let `k = log2(len)`. `queryMin(L, R) = min(table[L][k], table[R - 2^k + 1][k])`.
4. Instant O(1) query time because two overlapping power-of-two intervals fully cover `[L, R]`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace arr = [7, 2, 3, 0, 5, 10, 3, 12], Query Min in [1, 6]
traceSteps: Covering blocks: block1 starting at L=1 length 4 [indices 1..4: 2,3,0,5] -> min 0.
block2 ending at R=6 length 4 [indices 3..6: 0,5,10,3] -> min 0.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Answers Range Minimum Query (RMQ) in true O(1) constant time for static arrays.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When array elements never change and range min queries must be blazingly fast.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) via Euler Tour RMQ reduction.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(1) query time outperforms logarithmic Segment Trees.

algorithms.title: Sparse Table (Static Range Maximum Query)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log N) Precomputation, O(1) Query
algorithms.summary: Precomputes range maxima enabling instant O(1) constant time queries for static arrays.
explanation: 1. Sparse Table definition: `table[i][j]` stores maximum in range `[i, i + 2^j - 1]`.
2. Precomputation: `table[i][j] = max(table[i][j-1], table[i + 2^(j-1)][j-1])`.
3. Idempotent Query: Range [L, R] length `len = R - L + 1`. Let `k = log2(len)`. `queryMax(L, R) = max(table[L][k], table[R - 2^k + 1][k])`.
4. Instant O(1) query time because `max(max(A), max(B)) = max(A U B)`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace arr = [1, 5, 8, 2, 9, 3], Query Max in [1, 4]
traceSteps: block1 starting at L=1 length 4 [5, 8, 2, 9] -> max 9.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Answers Range Maximum Query in true O(1) constant time for static arrays.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding maximum values over static array ranges in O(1) time.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Peak signal amplitude identification, sliding dynamic boundary limits.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(1) query execution avoiding log N tree traversals.

algorithms.title: Sparse Table (Static Range GCD Query)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log N log(Max)) Precomputation, O(log(Max)) Query
algorithms.summary: Precomputes range GCDs enabling instant Range GCD queries for static arrays.
explanation: 1. Idempotent Property of GCD: `gcd(gcd(A), gcd(B)) = gcd(A U B)`.
2. Sparse Table construction: `table[i][j] = gcd(table[i][j-1], table[i + 2^(j-1)][j-1])`.
3. Range Query: `queryGCD(L, R) = gcd(table[L][k], table[R - 2^k + 1][k])` where `k = log2(R - L + 1)`.
4. Executes range GCD queries without tree traversals, taking time equal to a single GCD calculation.

exampleTrace.title: Trace arr = [12, 24, 36, 48, 60], Query GCD in [1, 3]
traceSteps: Result = gcd(12, 12) = 12 in O(1) table lookups.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes Range GCD over static arrays in single GCD evaluation time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When querying subarray GCDs frequently without element modifications.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Number theory sequence analysis, lattice alignment.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(1) table lookups + single GCD call beats Segment Tree log N tree traversals.
